name: Redis Lua
title: Redis Lua (Redis 8.0)

type.text: **The embedded dialect is documented command by command**: Redis ships one Lua 5.1 interpreter, and the Lua API reference names the libraries a script may use — `string`, `table`, `math`, `os.clock`, `struct`, `cjson`, `cmsgpack`, `bit`
**No static type check**: types are decided at run time, and a `nil` from a missing key becomes a fault only when the line that touches it executes
**Dispatch follows the run-time value**: `ipairs`, `table.insert`, and metatable `__index` chains resolve by what the value is when the call runs
**No sum types**: a result carries one value, and a script signals an alternative with a `nil`, a boolean flag, or a table convention
**No generic type parameter**: reusable script logic is copied between projects; a Functions library has no parameterised routine
**One global name space**: Lua globals default to the shared global table, and Redis runs scripts and functions in one Lua state, so name collisions are a deployment fact
**Operators are metatable dispatch**: `+`, `..`, and `#` on a table mean what its metatable says, so the call site's meaning follows the data
**nil is a value on every path**: a missing key's reply, an absent table field, and an unset global all reach expressions, and indexing nil raises mid-script
**`redis.call` shows the command, not the effect**: the script text names the command, not which keys it mutates, expires, or replicates
**The script-to-server boundary is unchecked**: `redis.call` enters the server's command dispatcher, and no check ties the command names, key arguments, and replies to the script's expectations

construction.text: **Atomic execution is the contract**: Redis runs the script to completion before serving any other client, so all of the script's effects commit together
**Globals persist across calls**: scripts run in one shared Lua state, and a global written by a script stays visible to the next call — avoiding globals is a published Redis scripting practice
**Nothing is immutable by default**: tables, `KEYS`, and `ARGV` are mutated in place, and function libraries share the state they mutate
**No constructor validates a shape**: a result table is assembled field by field, and a missing field surfaces as a `nil` on the reader's side
**Iteration order is the table's, not yours**: `pairs()` visits a hash-part table in an order the script cannot state
**One value, many names**: a table handed to `redis.call` and kept in a global is the same table, and Lua 5.1 source shows no aliasing declaration
**Key-space notifications react outside the script**: a script's writes fire subscribers and module consumers that the script text never mentions

memory.text: **Allocation is the interpreter's**: scripts create tables and strings, and Redis's bundled Lua collector reclaims them; no script frees memory
**The collector pauses the server**: Lua's collection work runs on the main thread during the script's run, so collecting a big table is a latency spike every client sees
**Scope does not release**: `__gc` runs when the collector decides, not at the end of a block, and a script cannot bind release to scope
**No ownership is expressed**: tables move through `redis.call` replies and globals with no owner, and the collector decides lifetime
**A runaway script holds its memory to the end**: `SCRIPT KILL` stops only a script that has not written, so a script past its write budget runs to completion

error.text: **No structured error path**: `error()` raises any value, `pcall` returns it untyped, and a script reporting 'insufficient funds' invents its own convention
**Failures nobody is required to handle**: `redis.call` on a wrong-type key raises, and a script with no `pcall` wrapper commits nothing and hands the fault to the client
**A failure can be ignored**: `pcall`'s false reply is discarded freely, and scripts commonly drop the flag
**No composable result type**: success values, nils, and raised strings share the return slot, so callers compose them by convention
**The fault boundary is one call**: a raised error aborts the script, the server keeps serving, and the blast radius is the current call

concurrency.text: **No parallel execution**: Redis runs one script at a time on its main thread, and every client waits for the script to finish
**Coroutines are unstructured**: Lua 5.1 `coroutine` transfers control by hand, and no construct scopes a running child
**Atomicity is total**: every effect commits before any other client runs, so a script needs no lock to compose a read-modify-write
**The budget is a wall**: `lua-time-limit` decides when a read-only script may be stopped, and a script that has written runs to the end

platform.text: **The language runs only inside Redis**: Redis ships a single embedded scripting engine, the Lua 5.1 interpreter, and the Functions docs name it as the only engine present
**A poor fit for general application logic**: scripts exchange replies with clients; HTTP, file I/O (the sandbox exposes `os.clock` only), and multi-pass algorithms belong to the client
**Redis 8 makes Functions engine-agnostic by design, and Lua 5.1 is the engine that ships**: more engines are a plan, not a feature

performance.text: **Bytecode interpretation, no JIT**: Redis bundles the Lua 5.1 interpreter, not LuaJIT, and a hot script loop pays per bytecode instruction
**Collector pauses are server latency**: Lua's GC steps run on the main thread, and a script's big tables appear as latency spikes in every client's timings
**Data locality is the point**: the script reads and writes inside the server, and the docs call scripting 'very efficient' because the data never leaves

ecosystem.text: **No package manager for scripts**: a Functions library embeds its full source, the sandbox exposes only the libraries Redis pre-imports, and nothing installs into the server's Lua
**Tooling fragments across clients**: `redis-cli --ldb`, the ZeroBrane Studio plugin, and the per-language client libraries cover scripting at different levels
**A niche within a niche**: Lua developers who write server-side Redis scripts are a small hiring pool
**RDB snapshots do not cross a version boundary backward**: a snapshot written by a newer Redis cannot be loaded by an older one, and Redis's knowledge base states it as the rule for upgrades
**The server is open source (AGPLv3 since Redis 8), and the Lua API, Functions, and persistence docs are public

evolution.text: **Script behavior moved under scripts**: Redis 7.0 shifted the recommended path from `EVAL` to Functions — changing how code is loaded, named, and persisted — and Redis 7.4 added eviction from the `EVAL` script cache
**The embedded dialect is frozen**: Redis ships the same Lua 5.1 line it has used since 2012; upstream Lua 5.4's changes — an integer subtype, a bitwise library, GC options — never reach scripts
**Scripts from Redis 2.6 run on Redis 8**: `EVAL` with `KEYS` and `ARGV` has kept its contract across the whole line

domain.text: **Adopting Redis Lua means adopting Redis**: scripts call the Redis command API, and the language exists to compose key operations on Redis data structures
Redis Lua is used to script server-side read-modify-write logic over stored data: conditional updates across keys commit atomically inside the server
**Cluster rules travel with the script**: every key a script touches must be an input key argument, and generated key names break cross-slot operation

learning.text: **The language core is small**: `local`, `for`, function values, and tables fit a short manual, and Redis's own design notes call Lua 'simple and easy to learn'
**Two domains at once**: a scripter needs Lua's table idioms and metatables, the Redis command API, the atomicity budget, and the key-argument rules together
**The sandbox's shape is a page of rules**: which globals exist, which `os` functions are exposed, and what `SCRIPT KILL` will stop

syntax.text: **Scripts read linearly**: a short Lua script is a statement list, and `redis.call` renders as a plain function call

**Lua 5.1's surface is uneven**: `table.insert(t, v)` against `table.concat(list, sep)`, methods as `('x'):rep(2)`, 1-based indexing, no `++`, no ternary — the idioms are conventions to learn one by one

testing.text: **No test harness ships with the language**: testing a script needs a running Redis, and every project wires its own harness; the debugger's forked sessions are for authoring, not CI
**The debugger reaches scripts, not Functions**: LDB steps, breakpoints, and variable inspection attach to `EVAL`, and the Functions docs name the debugger as the one capability functions lack
**Type faults surface only at execution**: `tonumber` on a malformed `ARGV` value, indexing nil, and a wrong-type key all resolve when the line runs
**No monotonic clock in the sandbox**: the `os` library exposes `os.clock` only, so elapsed-time tests read wall time

security.text: **Untrusted data enters untyped**: values read back from keys are data, and every arithmetic, concatenation, and pattern use re-checks its type at run time
**Embedding values in the script text is a documented abuse**: Redis's EVAL docs warn that value-embedded scripts generate a new script text on each call, and the parse follows the embedded value
**Arithmetic leaves the range in silence**: Lua 5.1 numbers are C doubles, integers past 2^53 lose precision quietly, and the `bit` library truncates to 32 bits by C cast
**Passing data as `ARGV` keeps values out of the parse**, and Redis's docs make it the rule
**ACL categories gate scripting**: the `@scripting` permission decides which clients may load and run scripts

reproducibility.text: **A script is source text**: the same text on the same Redis version and dataset reproduces the same result, and there is no build artifact
**Dependencies are not pinned**: applications ship scripts beside client code, and no manifest names the Redis version a script expects
**The distribution carries no toolchain pin for script code**: Redis bundles its Lua line inside the server, and a deployment has no machine-read pair of server version to script version

supplychain.text: **Published drivers carry no signed provenance by default**: `redis-py` on PyPI and `ioredis` on npm name their publishers, and a consumer must trust the package they install
**Registries carry namespaces**: PyPI and npm name each package's owner, so there is no flat namespace to hijack
**Advisories exist**: Redis publishes its CVE list for the server and stack components, and the GitHub advisory database covers the major Python and Node clients

observability.text: **No stable tracing and metrics standard is part of the language**: a script reports through `INFO` counters and the server's own telemetry
**No structured logging in the sandbox**: `redis.log` writes a message and level into the server's log format, and the debug console is debug-only
**The server names a slow script**: `SLOWLOG` records script executions past the latency threshold with their duration, and `SCRIPT KILL` is the documented stop path

feedback.text: **The edit-test loop is a text submission**: `redis-cli --eval /tmp/script.lua` runs a file with no build step
**Editors do not analyse Redis Lua**: `redis.call`'s command names and key semantics are checked by the server at execution, and no incremental analyser ships for the language
**LDB is a real debugger for scripts**: step, breakpoints, backtrace, variable print, and Redis command tracing ship in `redis-cli`

interop.text: **No foreign-function interface**: the sandbox exposes no C library, `os` is reduced to `os.clock`, and extending Redis in compiled code is a C module's job, outside the language
**No portable target**: scripts run on Redis's embedded engine and nowhere else
**The client boundary is the command API**: a script's reply converts to RESP, and every language's Redis client can call `EVAL`

governance.text: **Governance is Redis-owned**: the embedded engine, the Functions design, and script-cache behavior all follow Redis's roadmap, and a second engine is stated as a plan
**The engine is published**: Redis bundles its Lua line as open source in the server repository, and the Functions docs describe the engine interface

**Conformance is what Redis's Lua fork does**: the `redis.call` API, the library set, and the atomicity rules exist only in the server's implementation, and no shared test suite runs an independent implementation
**The parser is published**: Redis's bundled Lua source is the parser, readable and reusable by tooling

tradeoffs: **Code ownership: application-side (`EVAL`) versus server-side (Functions)**: scripts ship with the client code and reload after a restart, functions persist and replicate with the dataset — the server then carries application logic that the client no longer ships

**Script-cache economics**: `EVALSHA` keeps script text in the server, Redis's own docs warn that value-embedded scripts 'consume a large amount of memory over time', and Redis 7.4's LRU eviction means the cache budget now decides which scripts the next call must resend
**Cluster key discipline**: every key a script touches must arrive as an input argument, so scripts that derive key names from data are written out of clustered deployments

**One roundtrip buys atomic composition**: a conditional multi-key update ships as a single call with no lock and no client-side race, and the standing duty is reviewing every script for length, because Redis runs a writing script to completion
verdict: Redis Lua is coupling-heavy at the language level and cheap at the deployment level, and the two facts are the same fact. The language is a frozen Lua 5.1 line embedded in Redis's main thread: dynamic typing with no static check, one shared global state, an unchecked `redis.call` boundary, no parallel execution, no FFI, no package boundary, and silent numeric range exits in a language built on C doubles. What the embedding buys is real: atomic read-modify-write where the data lives, a published remote debugger for scripts, a documented CVE feed, and `EVAL` contracts that have held since Redis 2.6. Main strengths: atomic execution, data locality, LDB, tiny language core. Main weaknesses: the dialect is frozen, Functions run where no debugger reaches, RDB snapshots cross a release boundary unpromised backward, and the language runs only inside Redis.

energy.text: Runs on the Redis main thread: a long script is a server-wide latency spike, and the energy and time are the server's, not the script's.

ai-readiness.text: Lua 5.1 is small and richly represented in public code, and the Redis Lua API is documented command by command: current models write common scripts reliably, with the key-argument and atomicity rules needing review.

safety.text: No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

delivery.note: Redis persists Functions libraries with the dataset and caches EVAL scripts in the Lua state; no compiled unit crosses a producer boundary.

data_formats.note: The Redis knowledge base publishes both directions: newer Redis loads older RDB files, and older Redis cannot load RDB files created by newer versions; the Redis 7.2 feature-set note calls its RDB format incompatible with older versions.

The persistence docs publish that current Redis loads AOF logs written by older servers — truncated tails are discarded under `aof-load-truncated` — and the 7.0 multi-part format is the storage form the docs treat as current.
